messages.body_plain:
Hi Jane,

Thanks for your interest in the package!

After looking through your code, there are a few potential issues that I can spot. First, in the .stan file:

1) You should be estimating a hyper-location and hyper-scale parameter for the standard deviation of the normal model that you are using. Looking at line 58:

`scr[t, i] ~ normal(alpha + beta * ev, sigma[4]);`

Here, you are using sigma[4] as the standard deviation for the normal model, but the `sigma` vector (as is specified in the code) is the hyper-scale parameter for the model parameters. This is kind of confusing because the normal model has a parameter called sigma, but what you need to do is estimate a hyper-location and hyper-sigma for the "normal model sigma" just like any other parameter (e.g. the learning rate "A" has an estimated mean and sigma).

2) In the same chunk of code above, you had:

`scr[t, i] ~ normal(alpha + beta * ev, sigma[4]);`

but ev is a vector when it should be the ev of the chosen option (or received reward/punishment/etc.). This can be corrected by doing the following:

`scr[t, i] ~ normal(alpha + beta * ev[stim[t,i]], sigma[4]);`

3) You have modified the code so that parameters are estimated using a centered parameterization, but have not specified the parameter vectors correctly to reflect this difference. Our .stan codes are separating the location and scale hyper-parameters for each parameter estimate in order to make sampling more efficient. In making this change, it looks like you also removed the hierarchy between mu_alpha and mu_beta and the individual alpha and beta estimates and then estimated a single alpha and beta all subjects.

I have attached a .stan code that addresses all the potential issues above for your reference (with a few comments to help).

On the R code, I am a bit confused about the simulation code. The model doing the simulation is assuming that SCR is a results of the learned expectation, but in your .stan code it is modeled as part of a linear (`scr[t, i] ~ normal(alpha + beta * ev, sigma)`) model. To recover parameters, you will need to simulated data from the exact model as specified in the .stan code. This includes having individual parameters for alpha, beta, A, and sigma, and then simulating the task data with those parameters for each subject. If you find it easier, you can actually simulate data directly from the .stan code. I have never done this, but there are some tutorials online that show how to do so (e.g. http://modernstatisticalworkflow.blogspot.com/2017/04/an-easy-way-to-simulate-fake-data-from.html).

Anyway, I hope this helps! Let us know if you have questions about the .stan code I attached.

Best,
Nate

>

>
>       # value updating (learning)
>       ev[stim[t, i]] = ev[stim[t, i]] + A[i] * PE;
>     }
>   }
> }
>
> Thank you so much.
> Jane

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Nate, that was very helpful.

A few clarifications:

1. You are right the simulation; it is assuming that SCR is a result of learned expectation.
The reason I modeled it as a linear model in stan is because this is how I would have done it
in MLE. The learning model is the R-W-model, the observation model is a linear model of
the form y ~ N(alpha + beta * ev, sigma), where ev is the expected value (c.f. Daw 2011, p. 23).

2. I am thus not interested in alpha or beta per se, but only in A (and mu_A), the learning rate.

3. When I run the code with your modifications, it appears that the sampling gets stuck in
the warmup (at 20%) and never makes it to the next iteration. How would I proceed to debug
my model?

Thank you again!

messages.subject: Re: Reinforcement learning model with linear observation model
messages.subject_clean: Reinforcement learning model with linear observation model
messages.body_plain:
1. Yes, the model makes sense to me. My comment is that if you do not simulate the full model (RW + linear model), then you may have trouble recovering the true parameters when you fit the data to the full .stan model. The way the data are simulated now assumes that alpha == 0, beta == 1, and sigma == 0 (since scr == ev, so there is no residual error after the ev is computed). My confusion was coming from me assuming that you would want to simulate the whole model, but if not then I understand now.

2. If you are interested in how well you can recover learning rates in real data, I would recommend also simulating alpha, beta, and sigma parameters. That way, you have a sense of how well you can recover the learning rates that you will interpret when you fit the full model to the real data.

3. Interesting that it is sticking at 20%. Are there any error/warning messages that you get? I have never run into a problem where the chains stop running part-way through–if they get stuck for a long period of time, it is typically safe to assume that the model/data entered into the model have been mis-specified. One thing you may try is to run it with very few iterations (e.g. 10 or 20 with 5 or 10 warmup). If it still gets stuck, I wonder if it has something to do with the data being sent to Stan?

Best,
Nate

messages.body_plain:
Of course!

Yes, it could have potentially been that there was no variation in the responses (i.e. if the learning rate is known, the responses are completely determined). In practice, I typically do something like:

alpha  = rnorm(10, mean = 0.5, sd = 0.1)

beta = rnorm(10, mean = 1, sd = 0.2)

...

to generate individual level parameters (for 10 subjects in this case), and then use these to simulate the task data. Better yet, you would then add error to each individual-level parameter. After generating these parameters, then for your sampling statement it would be like:

scr = rnorm(1, mean = alpha[subject] + beta[subject] * ev[choice], sd = sigma_er[choice])

The SCR will be randomly distributed around the linear model as it will be in reality.

Hopefully this helps!

Best,

Nate

messages.subject: Drift Diffusion Model
messages.subject_clean: Drift Diffusion Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am very interested in applying the drift diffusion model.  According to my understanding, the input for the model for each trial includes subject identifier, response, and reaction time, but does not include any information about the stimulus/trial type.  In my task, there are two stimuli and two responses; subjects are instructed to respond based on the stimulus.  An "A" response to an "A" stimulus would be correct, while a "B" response to an "A" stimulus would be an error.  The accuracy rates on this task are quite high, with many subjects achieving 100% accuracy.

I have been unable to apply the hBayesDM drift diffusion model to my data.  If I encode an "A" response as the upper boundary and a "B" response as the lower boundary, the model will not generate results (presumably because, without information about the stimulus type, the resulting drift rate would be approximately zero and all responses would be based on noise).  If I encode a correct response as the upper boundary and an error as the lower boundary, the model will not run, presumably because many subjects have 100% accuracy (i.e. no error trials).

Is it possible to apply the drift diffusion model to my task?

Thank you,
Jon

messages.subject: Re: Reinforcement learning model with linear observation model
messages.subject_clean: Reinforcement learning model with linear observation model
messages.body_plain:
One thing I might point out is that I think you should be simulating sigma_er in a different way. Right now, you are generating "gaussian noise", and then just adding it to the estimated value. Instead, you should be generating a positive sigma_er for each subject, and then simulating the response like this:

`
# beta and noise
alpha <- truncnorm::rtruncnorm(nsubs, mean=0.4, sd=0.12, a=0, b=1)
beta0 <- rnorm(nsubs, mean=2.5, sd=0.2)
beta1 <- rnorm(nsubs, mean=1.2, sd=0.4)
sigma_er <- truncnorm::rtruncnorm(nsubs, mean=?, sd=?, a=0.05, b=Inf) # replace ? with what you think would be best

# create time series
for (i in 1:nsubs) {
  vm    <- vector("numeric", 35)
  vp    <- vector("numeric", 34)
  vm[1] <- 0.5
  vp[1] <- 0.5
  pc    <- 0
  mc    <- 0
  for (t in 1:(ntrials-1)) {
    if (stim[t] == 1) {
      mc       <- mc + 1
      vm[mc+1] <- vm[mc] + alpha[i] * (lambda[t] - vm[mc])
    } else if (pc < length(vp)-1) {
      pc       <- pc + 1
      vp[pc+1] <- vp[pc] + alpha[i] * (lambda[t] - vp[pc])
    }
  }
  y[stim==1] <- vm
  y[stim==2] <- vp

  # create final time series
  # corrupted by gaussian noise --> the "noise" here is actually estimated (i.e. it is the error after predicting the SCR given the expectation)
  y          <- rnorm(1, mean = beta0[i] + beta1[i] * y,  sd = sigma_er[i])
  Y[, i]     <- y

}
`

Note that I am using the `truncnorm` package above to simulate from a truncated normal distribution (learning rate must be between 0 and 1 and sigma_er must be above 0).

Best,
Nate

Jane,

Great! I am glad we could help. The individual parameters shrinking toward the average is the hierarchical shrinkage–in practice this shrinkage typically gives us better estimates than we would have without it (i.e. "regularized" estimates). Are the true individual rates at least within the 95% highest density interval of the estimated individual posteriors? Most of them should be.

Anyway, good luck with your project!

Best,

Nate

That was really helpful. I think it is working now. The model converges
and I can recover the average learning rate, althought the individual
learning rates sometimes appear to be too close to the average
compared to the simulated value.

Anyway, for completeness, this is the sampling code that I ended
up using:

for (i in 1:nsubs) {
  vm    <- 0.5
  vp    <- 0.5
  for (t in 1:ntrials) {
    if (stim[t] == 1) {
      v[t, i] <- vm
      vm <- vm + alpha[i] * (lambda[t] - vm)
    } else {
      v[t, i] <- vp
      vp <- vp + alpha[i] * (lambda[t] - vp)
    }
    mu <- beta0[i] + beta1[i] * v[t, i]
    Y[t, i] <- rnorm(1, mean=mu, sd=sigma[i])
  }
}

And attached is the output, comparing true individual learning rates
with the ones obtained from stan.

bimodal posteriors in the individual learning rates in a slightly more
complex model, and found your post on the different priors very helpful.
However, it looks like you decided to stick with the cauchy(0, 5) prior
in most of the models I saw. As you know, bimodal posteriors in individual
learning rates are a problem when we want to generate fMRI regressors
based on point estimates.

Would be very interested to hear your thoughts on this.

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jane,

Typically I find that the model is mis-specified or there are not enough observations at the individual level when I get this behavior. That said, I have tried versions with sigma ~ cauchy(0,1), which tends to help is most situations–I would try that first. If this still fails, you can try putting normal priors on the sigma (e.g. sigma ~ normal(0,5)).

If you still have trouble after this, it may be one of the problems above (i.e. mis-specification or too few observations at individual level).

Best,

Nate
